text: Future projections in the 2040–2050 timeframe came from multiple literature sources. Jet A demand assumes continued air travel growth. In a low scenario, SAF demand reflects existing mandates, while its future production potential depends on feedstock availability of both biomass and electricity. Hydrogen demand is based on energy system models that minimize costs under different policy scenarios, including net-zero pathways. LNG existing and future production assume the current natural gas liquefaction rate. Ethane projections reflect overall supply, as it is not typically used in cryogenic form. The Jet A, SAF, and hydrogen data is global whereas the LNG and ethane data are domestic. SAF, when blended with Jet A, is a drop-in fuel compatible with existing infrastructure and aircraft. It has been commercially available since 2016, with a sharp increase in production facilities since late 2024. Nearly all SAF is produced from fats, oils, and greases via the hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA) production pathway, but other pathways exist and still more are under development. The first commercial alcohol-to-jet plant started production in late 2025 (Epstein 2025). U.S. consumption rose from 26 million gallons in 2023 to 281 million gallons in 2025, but SAF still accounts for only about 1% of total jet fuel use (EPA 2025a, EIA 2025d). Expanding beyond HEFA—particularly to power-to-liquid (PtL) e-SAF—will depend on access to low-cost, low-carbon-free electricity. Cryogenic fuel use in aviation requires new aircraft design and different distribution, storage, and dispensing equipment. The feasibility of cryogenic fuel use for aviation applications is based on fuel physical, chemical, and thermal properties, engineering requirements for safe onboard storage and delivery, and performance impacts associated with the new cryogenic-fueled aircraft designs. To maintain LH , LNG, and LE below their respective boiling points, insulated storage 2 tanks capable of maintaining low temperatures and accommodating internal pressure rise due to heat ingress are required. Storage tank design and materials can vary by cryogenic fuel type impacting tank weight. For each of the cryogenic fuels discussed in this report, airport fueling installations and aircraft would need major adaptations, including vacuum-insulated storage tanks, cryogenic-rated transfer equipment, and strict safety protocols.
